---
title: "Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation"
---

The Bayesian chapters introduced [posterior predictive distributions](../statistical-inference/predictive-distributions.qmd) and [importance sampling](../statistical-inference/importance-sampling.qmd). The [leave-one-out page](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd) then defined prediction for an omitted observation. PSIS-LOO combines these ideas to approximate Bayesian leave-one-out prediction without fitting every omitted-data posterior directly.

A Bayesian model supplies a posterior distribution over parameter values rather than one fitted parameter vector. The predictive density of an omitted judgment should therefore be averaged over the posterior that would have been obtained without that judgment. Literal refitting carries out this instruction, but a model with $N$ observations would require $N$ additional posterior computations.

[**Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO)**](https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html) approximates those omitted-data posteriors using draws from the posterior fit to all observations.

## Beginning with exact Bayesian leave-one-out prediction

Let $y_{-i}$ denote all observed responses except $y_i$. If the prior is $p(\theta)$, the leave-one-out posterior is

$$
p(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
p(\theta)
\prod_{j\neq i}p(y_j\mid\theta).
$$

The exact leave-one-out predictive density for the omitted response is

$$
p(y_i\mid y_{-i})
=
\int
p(y_i\mid\theta)
p(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

This expression averages the likelihood of the omitted response over uncertainty in $\theta$ after fitting only the other responses. Taking logs and summing gives a leave-one-out estimate of the [**expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD)**](https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html):

$$
\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{loo}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\log p(y_i\mid y_{-i}).
$$

Larger values indicate greater predictive density for the omitted observations. Since log densities are often negative, a value of $-300$ is larger than $-320$.

## Relating the omitted posterior to the full posterior

Suppose we already have draws $\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}$ from the full posterior

$$
p(\theta\mid y)
\propto
p(\theta)
\prod_{j=1}^{N}p(y_j\mid\theta).
$$

Removing the $i$th likelihood term gives

$$
p(\theta\mid y_{-i})
\propto
\frac{p(\theta\mid y)}{p(y_i\mid\theta)}.
$$

Thus, a full-posterior draw receives a large raw importance ratio for the leave-one-out posterior when $p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})$ is small:

$$
r_i^{(s)}
\propto
\frac{1}{p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})}.
$$

This inverse weighting is both the computational shortcut and its potential weakness. If a few draws receive extremely large ratios, the full posterior may represent the omitted posterior poorly.

## Smoothing the largest ratios

PSIS fits a generalized Pareto distribution to the upper tail of the raw importance ratios and replaces the most extreme ratios with smoothed values. The approximation still uses the full-posterior draws, but no longer lets a few unstable raw values determine the estimate unchecked.

The [**Pareto $k$ diagnostic**](https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html) reports the fitted tail-shape parameter for each omitted observation. A larger $k$ suggests that the upper tail is heavy and that a few draws dominate the approximation. Thus, Pareto $k$ evaluates the computation used to estimate the omitted predictive density. It is not an optional decoration on the final score.

A large value does not prove that the observation should be removed. The observation may identify a model failure, a data error, or a region with little training support. It may instead show only that full-posterior draws are a poor proposal for the omitted posterior. These possibilities require inspecting the observation and, when necessary, performing a more reliable refit.

## Preserving the pointwise log likelihood

The `loo` package expects a matrix with one row per posterior draw and one column per pointwise likelihood contribution.

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Rows index posterior draws. Columns index observations.
dim(log_lik_draws)

loo_result <- loo::loo(log_lik_draws)
print(loo_result)

pareto_k <- loo::pareto_k_values(loo_result)
plot(pareto_k, ylab = "Pareto k")
```

Each matrix entry must be the log likelihood for one observation conditional on one posterior draw. A vector containing one total log likelihood per draw is not enough because omission operates one contribution at a time.

When a Pareto $k$ value is problematic, possible responses include exact refitting for that observation, moment matching, or a validation design that better matches the predictive question. The choice depends on whether the difficulty lies in the approximation, the fitted model, or the prediction task.

## Matching the omitted unit to the claim

Default PSIS-LOO omits one likelihood contribution. In repeated linguistic data, that contribution is often one trial. Other trials from the same participant and item remain in the posterior fit.

This procedure may answer a new-trial question. It does not automatically estimate prediction for a wholly new participant, item, verb, passage, or language. If the scientific claim concerns a new passage, all positions in one passage must be omitted together or the model must be refit under an equivalent grouped scheme.

Summing row-level PSIS-LOO values within a passage does not retroactively remove that passage from training. The likelihood partition and validation procedure must already hold out the complete group required by the predictive question.

## Checking the approximation

1. Which posterior appears in the exact predictive density $p(y_i\mid y_{-i})$?
2. Why are the raw importance ratios proportional to $1/p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})$?
3. What does Pareto $k$ diagnose?
4. What does a large Pareto $k$ not establish about an observation?
5. Why must the log-likelihood matrix retain one column per pointwise contribution?
6. Why can row-level PSIS-LOO fail to answer a new-speaker question?

## What PSIS-LOO establishes

PSIS-LOO approximates omitted-observation predictive density while averaging over posterior uncertainty. The Pareto $k$ diagnostic evaluates whether draws from the full posterior can represent each omitted posterior well enough for that approximation. The resulting score remains tied to the unit represented by one likelihood contribution.

The [next page](waic.qmd) uses the same pointwise log-likelihood matrix to construct a different approximation based on posterior variation.
